## Getting started

In R we use **dplyr** for tables and **ggplot2** for plots. In Python we use **NumPy** for arrays, **pandas** for tables, and **seaborn/matplotlib** for plots. These tools cover similar tasks, but their syntax and defaults differ.

Install packages once in your environment; load or import them in each new session. Run the examples in order so that objects created earlier are available. Occasionally restart your R or Python session and rerun the code to check that it does not depend on old objects.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```r
# Run once if needed:
# install.packages(c("dplyr", "ggplot2"))

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

### Python

```python
# Run once in a terminal if needed:
# python -m pip install numpy pandas matplotlib seaborn

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
```
:::

## Vectors and arithmetic

### Add one to every value

Use an R vector or a NumPy array for elementwise arithmetic. A Python list is a different container: `values + [1]` appends an element, and `values * 2` repeats the list.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```r
values <- c(10, 20, 30)
values + 1
# 11 21 31
values ^ 2
# 100 400 900
```

### Python

```python
values = np.array([10, 20, 30])
values + 1
# array([11, 21, 31])
values ** 2
# array([100, 400, 900])
```
:::

### Repeating a shorter vector

R **recycles** a shorter vector. NumPy **broadcasts** compatible shapes. Arrays of lengths four and two are not compatible, so make repetition explicit when that is what you intend.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```r
c(1, 2, 3, 4) + c(10, 20)
# 11 22 13 24
```

### Python

```python
np.array([1, 2, 3, 4]) + np.tile([10, 20], 2)
# array([11, 22, 13, 24])
```
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Compare the right containers"}
R atomic vectors and ordinary NumPy arrays have a common element type. A Python list can hold different types. NumPy can also hold arbitrary objects with `dtype=object`, but that does not give ordinary numeric-array behavior.
:::

## Indexing and keeping dimensions

### Select the first three values

R starts counting at **1**. Python starts at **0**, and a slice excludes its stop. R's `values[-1]` excludes the first element; Python's `values[-1]` selects the last.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```r
letters_example <- c("a", "b", "c", "d")
letters_example[1:3]
# "a" "b" "c"
letters_example[-1]
# "b" "c" "d"
```

### Python

```python
letters_example = np.array(["a", "b", "c", "d"])
letters_example[0:3]
# array(['a', 'b', 'c'])
letters_example[1:]
# array(['b', 'c', 'd'])
```
:::

### Keep a single row as a matrix

An integer index can remove a dimension. Use `drop = FALSE` in R, or a slice in NumPy, to keep it.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```r
m <- rbind(c(1, 2), c(3, 4))
m[1, ]                 # vector of length 2
m[1, , drop = FALSE]   # 1 × 2 matrix
m[, 2, drop = FALSE]   # 2 × 1 matrix
```

### Python

```python
m = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
m[0, :]     # shape (2,)
m[0:1, :]   # shape (1, 2)
m[:, 1:2]   # shape (2, 1)
```
:::

For a pandas table, `.iloc[0]` selects the first row as a Series; `.iloc[[0]]` keeps a one-row DataFrame. `.iloc` selects by position, while `.loc` selects by label. In particular, a `.loc` label slice includes its stop label. A pandas Series also aligns arithmetic by **index labels**, so two Series do not necessarily combine by position as NumPy arrays do.

## Missing values

### Calculate a mean when one value is missing

This difference can change a result without producing an error. R's `mean()` retains missingness by default; pandas `.mean()` skips missing values by default.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```r
measurements <- c(1, NA, 3)
mean(measurements)                 # NA
mean(measurements, na.rm = TRUE)   # 2
is.na(measurements)                # FALSE TRUE FALSE
```

### Python

```python
measurements = pd.Series([1, np.nan, 3])
measurements.mean(skipna=False)   # nan
measurements.mean()               # 2.0
measurements.isna()               # False, True, False
```
:::

NumPy's `np.mean()` propagates `np.nan`; `np.nanmean()` ignores it. Use `pd.isna()` or `.isna()` to detect missing data rather than equality tests. Nullable pandas columns can use `pd.NA`, whose behavior differs from `np.nan` in some operations.

`NULL` in R and `None` in Python represent absence, rather than an ordinary recorded measurement. `c(NULL, "a")` has one element, whereas `[None, "a"]` has two. Do not assume these values can be substituted without changing the data structure.

## Working with tables

### Read the same CSV

Both examples read the same used-car CSV directly from the course repository. Reading from a web address requires an internet connection. You can also download the file once and replace the address with its local path.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```r
data_url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stat-lu/dataviz/main/data/us_cars.csv"
cars <- read.csv(data_url)
head(cars)
nrow(cars)   # 2499
```

### Python

```python
data_url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stat-lu/dataviz/main/data/us_cars.csv"
cars = pd.read_csv(data_url)
cars.head()
len(cars)   # 2499
```
:::

### Filter rows and select columns

Select Tennessee cars from 2015 onwards, keeping their brand and price. dplyr interprets bare names as columns inside `filter()` and `select()`. pandas uses explicitly selected columns and a logical mask.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```r
recent <- filter(cars, state == "tennessee", year >= 2015)
select(recent, brand, price)
```

### Python

```python
keep = (cars["state"] == "tennessee") & (cars["year"] >= 2015)
recent = cars.loc[keep]
recent[["brand", "price"]]
```
:::

For pandas column conditions, use `&`, `|`, and `~` for and, or, and not. Put parentheses around each comparison. Python's `and`, `or`, and `not` expect single truth values. Use `.isin([...])` for membership of each value in a set, corresponding to R's `%in%`.

### Add a column and summarize groups

First calculate a price in thousands of dollars, then calculate each country's median price and number of listings. A group size counts rows; a nonmissing-value count may be smaller.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```r
cars_with_price <- mutate(cars, price_thousands = price / 1000)
grouped <- group_by(cars_with_price, country)
summarize(grouped,
          median_price = median(price_thousands, na.rm = TRUE),
          number_of_cars = n())
```

### Python

```python
cars_with_price = cars.assign(price_thousands=cars["price"] / 1000)
grouped = cars_with_price.groupby("country")
grouped.agg(
    median_price=("price_thousands", "median"),
    number_of_cars=("price_thousands", "size"),
)
```
:::

`mutate()` and `.assign()` return results to save. In Python, `other = cars` makes another name for the **same** table; assigning `other["price"] = ...` also changes `cars`. Use `cars.copy()` when you need an independent table. Avoid chained assignment such as `cars[keep]["price"] = ...`; select and assign explicitly with `.loc`.

### Express a sequence of operations

Once the individual operations are familiar, pipes and method chains can make a sequence easier to read. Intermediate objects remain useful when inspecting your work.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```r
cars %>%
  filter(color == "black") %>%
  group_by(state) %>%
  summarize(mean_mileage = mean(mileage, na.rm = TRUE),
            number_of_cars = n()) %>%
  arrange(mean_mileage)
```

### Python

```python
(
    cars.loc[cars["color"] == "black"]
    .groupby("state", as_index=False)
    .agg(mean_mileage=("mileage", "mean"),
         number_of_cars=("mileage", "size"))
    .sort_values("mean_mileage")
)
```
:::

## Categories and their order

Category order matters for axes and legends. Ordinary strings do not specify a meaningful order. Use an ordered factor in R or an ordered pandas categorical column.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```r
improvement <- factor(c("Marked", "None", "Some"),
                      levels = c("None", "Some", "Marked"),
                      ordered = TRUE)
```

### Python

```python
improvement = pd.Categorical(
    ["Marked", "None", "Some"],
    categories=["None", "Some", "Marked"],
    ordered=True,
)
```
:::

CSV files do not store factor levels or category order. Restore them after import by specifying the categories and their order explicitly. You usually do not need the historical `stringsAsFactors` defaults to solve this task: specify the categories you need explicitly.

## Plotting the same data

Let's plot city against highway fuel economy using **ggplot2's** `mpg` dataset. Python reads a CSV copy from Rdatasets, which also makes R datasets available outside R. A dataset with the same name in another library can contain different variables.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```r
mpg_data <- ggplot2::mpg

ggplot(mpg_data, aes(cty, hwy)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(x = "City fuel economy (mpg)",
       y = "Highway fuel economy (mpg)")
```

### Python

```python
mpg_url = "https://vincentarelbundock.github.io/Rdatasets/csv/ggplot2/mpg.csv"
mpg_data = pd.read_csv(mpg_url).drop(columns="rownames")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 4))
sns.scatterplot(data=mpg_data, x="cty", y="hwy", alpha=0.6, ax=ax)
ax.set(xlabel="City fuel economy (mpg)",
       ylabel="Highway fuel economy (mpg)")
plt.show()
```
:::

The data-to-aesthetic decisions are the same; the plotting APIs differ. ggplot2 combines a grammar of graphics into a plot object. With matplotlib, functions add artists to axes; seaborn provides convenient statistical plotting functions on top of it. Check defaults: for example, a seaborn line plot may estimate a mean unless you specify `estimator=None`. For repeated measurements, use `units` to identify each subject and `estimator=None` to draw a separate line for each one.

## Functions and matrices

### Define a function

Python marks a function body with indentation and needs an explicit `return`. R returns its final expression. Default argument expressions in R are evaluated when needed during a call; Python evaluates defaults when the function is defined.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```r
square_sum <- function(a, b = 1) {
  (a + b)^2
}
square_sum(2)   # 9
```

### Python

```python
def square_sum(a, b=1):
    return (a + b) ** 2

square_sum(2)   # 9
```
:::

If a Python function needs a fresh list for each call, use a `None` default and create the list in the body:

```python
def add_item(item, items=None):
    if items is None:
        items = []
    items.append(item)
    return items
```

### Multiply matrices

Distinguish elementwise multiplication from matrix multiplication. In both examples, the matrices have the same rows and columns.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```r
A <- rbind(c(1, 2), c(3, 4))
B <- rbind(c(2, 0), c(0, 2))
A * B     # elementwise
A %*% B   # matrix multiplication
```

### Python

```python
A = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
B = np.array([[2, 0], [0, 2]])
A * B   # elementwise
A @ B   # matrix multiplication
```
:::

## Where to go next

Practice with the **Cars** examples first: filter, select, mutate, group, and summarize. Then compare a plot of the same data in both languages. Before trusting that the results agree, check the selected rows, missing-value handling, units, category order, and statistical summaries.

For detailed reference, use the official [pandas comparison with R](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/getting_started/comparison/comparison_with_r.html), [NumPy indexing guide](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/user/basics.indexing.html), and [R extraction documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/Extract.html).

This handout presents copyable examples to run in an R or Python session. Its editable source is `r-python.qmd`. [Quarto](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/html-basics.html) provides the language tabs, syntax highlighting, and copy buttons.
